subproblem.title: Hausdorff measure on a cone: spheres are null and |x|^α is integrable near 0 (α > −m) and near ∞ (β < −m)
subproblem.statement: Let P, m ∈ ℕ and M ⊆ ℝ^P with 0 ∉ M, closure(M) ⊆ M ∪ {0}, tx ∈ M for all x ∈ M and t > 0, and H^m(M ∩ K) < ∞ for every compact K (H^m = μHE[m]). Then (a) H^m(M ∩ {|x| = c}) = 0 for every c > 0; (b) ∫⁻_{M ∩ {|x| < 1}} ofReal(|x|^α) dH^m < ∞ for every real α > −m; (c) ∫⁻_{M ∖ {|x| < 1}} ofReal(|x|^β) dH^m < ∞ for every real β < −m (real powers).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P m : ℕ) (M : Set (Euclid P)), (0 : Euclid P) ∉ M → closure M ⊆ insert 0 M → (∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → ∀ x ∈ M, t • x ∈ M) → (∀ K : Set (Euclid P), IsCompact K → μHE[m] (M ∩ K) ≠ ∞) → (∀ c : ℝ, 0 < c → μHE[m] (M ∩ sphere (0 : Euclid P) c) = 0) ∧ (∀ α : ℝ, -(m : ℝ) < α → ∫⁻ x in M ∩ ball (0 : Euclid P) 1, ENNReal.ofReal (‖x‖ ^ α) ∂μHE[m] ≠ ∞) ∧ (∀ β : ℝ, β < -(m : ℝ) → ∫⁻ x in M \ ball (0 : Euclid P) 1, ENNReal.ofReal (‖x‖ ^ β) ∂μHE[m] ≠ ∞)
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source. Parent proof (0e)(i)–(iii) and the finiteness part of step 6 ("Finiteness (replacing the use of (5))"). These replace the printed polar formula (5) of the proof of B.2 by dyadic scaling of H^m (documented departure (i) of the parent proof).

Notation. μ := μHE[m]; r(x) := |x|; A(a, b) := {x : a ≤ r(x) < b} for 0 < a < b. All sets used below are Borel.

1. (tM = M.) Let t > 0. tM ⊆ M by the cone property. If x ∈ M then t⁻¹x ∈ M and x = t(t⁻¹x) ∈ tM. Hence tM = M, and for every S ⊆ ℝ^P, M ∩ tS = t(M ∩ S) (if y = ts ∈ M with s ∈ S, then s = t⁻¹y ∈ M).

2. (M is Borel.) M = closure(M) ∖ {0}. Indeed M ⊆ closure(M), and 0 ∉ M. Conversely, if x ∈ closure(M) and x ≠ 0, then x ∈ closure(M) ⊆ M ∪ {0}, so x ∈ M. A closed set minus a point is Borel.

3. (Scaling.) By definition (euclideanHausdorffMeasure_def), μ = c·μH[m] for a constant c ∈ (0, ∞). For t > 0 and every S ⊆ ℝ^P, μH[m](tS) = t^m·μH[m](S) (Mathlib Measure.hausdorffMeasure_smul₀, MeasureTheory/Measure/Hausdorff.lean:753, with d = m ≥ 0 and r = t ≠ 0). Hence μ(tS) = t^m·μ(S). With step 1, μ(M ∩ tS) = t^m·μ(M ∩ S).

4. (Dyadic annuli.) Let a₀ := μ(M ∩ A(1, 2)). Then a₀ ≤ μ(M ∩ closedBall(0, 2)) < ∞ by the local finiteness hypothesis, closedBall(0, 2) being compact. For k ∈ ℤ, A(2^k, 2^{k+1}) = 2^k·A(1, 2). So by step 3, μ(M ∩ A(2^k, 2^{k+1})) = 2^{km}·a₀.

5. (Part (a): spheres are null.) For c > 0 put S_c := M ∩ sphere(0, c). sphere(0, c) = c·sphere(0, 1), so μ(S_c) = c^m·μ(S_1) by step 3. For c ∈ [1, 2] the sets S_c are pairwise disjoint Borel subsets of M ∩ closedBall(0, 2), whose measure B is finite (step 4). For c ≥ 1, μ(S_c) ≥ μ(S_1). Suppose μ(S_1) > 0. Choose N ∈ ℕ with N·μ(S_1) > B and distinct c_1, …, c_N ∈ [1, 2]. Then B ≥ μ(S_{c_1} ∪ … ∪ S_{c_N}) = Σ_i μ(S_{c_i}) ≥ N·μ(S_1) > B, a contradiction. So μ(S_1) = 0, and μ(S_c) = c^m·0 = 0 for every c > 0.

6. (Part (b).) Let α > −m. Every x ∈ M has 0 < r(x) because 0 ∉ M. So M ∩ ball(0, 1) is the disjoint union over k ≥ 1 of the Borel sets M ∩ A(2^{−k}, 2^{1−k}). On A(2^{−k}, 2^{1−k}), r^α ≤ 2^{|α|}·2^{−kα}: if α ≥ 0, r^α < (2^{1−k})^α = 2^α·2^{−kα}; if α < 0, r^α ≤ (2^{−k})^α = 2^{−kα}. The lower integral is countably additive over disjoint measurable pieces, and the pieces have measure 2^{−km}a₀ (step 4). Hence
 ∫⁻_{M ∩ ball(0,1)} ofReal(r^α) dμ ≤ Σ_{k≥1} 2^{|α|}·2^{−kα}·2^{−km}·a₀ = 2^{|α|}·a₀·Σ_{k≥1} (2^{−(m+α)})^k < ∞,
a geometric series with ratio 2^{−(m+α)} < 1 (m + α > 0).

7. (Part (c).) Let β < −m. M ∖ ball(0, 1) is the disjoint union over k ≥ 0 of the sets M ∩ A(2^k, 2^{k+1}). On A(2^k, 2^{k+1}), r^β ≤ 2^{|β|}·2^{kβ}, by the same case distinction as in step 6. Hence
 ∫⁻_{M ∖ ball(0,1)} ofReal(r^β) dμ ≤ Σ_{k≥0} 2^{|β|}·2^{kβ}·2^{km}·a₀ = 2^{|β|}·a₀·Σ_{k≥0} (2^{m+β})^k < ∞,
since 2^{m+β} < 1. ∎
proof_key_steps: tM = M for t > 0, and M = closure(M) ∖ {0} is Borel.
H^m(tS) = t^m H^m(S) (hausdorffMeasure_smul₀), so H^m(M ∩ {2^k ≤ |x| < 2^{k+1}}) = 2^{km}a₀ with a₀ < ∞.
The spheres M ∩ {|x| = c}, c ∈ [1,2], are disjoint in a finite-measure set and have measure c^m·H^m(M ∩ {|x| = 1}), so that measure is 0.
Dyadic decomposition and geometric series Σ 2^{−k(m+α)} (k ≥ 1) and Σ 2^{k(m+β)} (k ≥ 0) give the two finiteness statements.

subproblem.title: Rademacher's theorem on an embedded C¹ submanifold: locally Lipschitz functions are differentiable within M at H^m-a.e. point
subproblem.statement: Let P, m ∈ ℕ, M ⊆ ℝ^P an embedded C¹ m-dimensional submanifold (IsEmbeddedSubmanifold 1 m M) and f : ℝ^P → ℝ locally Lipschitz on M. Then for μHE[m]⌞M-almost every x, f is differentiable within M at x.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P m : ℕ) (M : Set (Euclid P)) (f : Euclid P → ℝ), IsEmbeddedSubmanifold 1 m M → LocallyLipschitzOn M f → ∀ᵐ x ∂(μHE[m].restrict M), DifferentiableWithinAt ℝ f M x
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source. Parent proof (0g): "A locally Lipschitz function on M is differentiable within M at H^m-a.e. point of M (Rademacher's theorem in the coordinates of the graph charts, Simon 2, 4.8–4.9: G is locally Lipschitz, so it maps L^m-null sets to H^m-null sets)". Here the given C¹ charts are used directly. A local left inverse comes from the inverse function theorem (Simon 2, 4.4).

Notation. μ := μHE[m]. A chart is a triple (V, W, ψ) as in IsEmbeddedSubmanifold 1 m M: V ⊆ ℝ^m and W ⊆ ℝ^P open; ψ C¹ on V and injective on V; ψ(V) = W ∩ M; V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) compact for every compact K ⊆ W; Dψ(z) injective for every z ∈ V.

1. (Charts are homeomorphisms onto W ∩ M.) Let (V, W, ψ) be a chart, b ∈ V, and let y_k ∈ W ∩ M with y_k → ψ(b). Write y_k = ψ(b_k) with b_k ∈ V. Then b_k → b. Indeed, K := {y_k} ∪ {ψ(b)} is compact and contained in W, so all b_k lie in the compact set V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K). Every cluster point b' of (b_k) lies in V and satisfies ψ(b') = ψ(b) by continuity of ψ on V, so b' = b by injectivity.

2. (M is Borel.) For each y ∈ M fix a chart (V_y, W_y, ψ_y) with y ∈ W_y, and let O := ⋃_y W_y (open, M ⊆ O). We claim M = O ∩ closure(M). Let p ∈ O ∩ closure(M), say p ∈ W_y. Then p is a limit of points y_k ∈ M ∩ W_y = ψ_y(V_y). The set K := {y_k} ∪ {p}, for k large, is a compact subset of W_y. By properness the preimages b_k lie in a compact subset of V_y, so a subsequence converges to some b ∈ V_y with ψ_y(b) = p. Hence p ∈ M. So M is Borel. Since ℝ^P is second countable (Lindelöf), there are countably many charts (V_i, W_i, ψ_i), i ∈ ℕ, with M ⊆ ⋃_i W_i.

3. (Local left inverse.) Fix a chart (V, W, ψ) and a ∈ V; let L := Dψ(a), injective. Let Q : ℝ^P → ℝ^m be a linear map with Q∘L = id; e.g. Q := (L*L)⁻¹L*, where L*L is invertible because L is injective. Φ := Q∘ψ is C¹ on the open set V, hence strictly differentiable at a, with DΦ(a) = id. By the inverse function theorem (Mathlib HasStrictFDerivAt.localInverse and its properties) there are an open V₀ with a ∈ V₀ ⊆ V, an open U₀ ∋ Φ(a), and a map Θ : ℝ^m → ℝ^m, differentiable at Φ(a), with Φ(V₀) ⊆ U₀ and Θ(Φ(b)) = b for all b ∈ V₀.

4. (A neighbourhood of ψ(a) in M lies in ψ(V₀).) There is δ > 0 with M ∩ ball(ψ(a), δ) ⊆ ψ(V₀) ∩ W. Otherwise there are y_k ∈ M ∖ ψ(V₀) with y_k → ψ(a). For large k, y_k ∈ W ∩ M (W is open), so y_k = ψ(b_k) with b_k ∈ V. By step 1, b_k → a, so b_k ∈ V₀ for large k, a contradiction.

5. (Transfer of differentiability.) Let g := f∘ψ. For y ∈ M ∩ ball(ψ(a), δ), write y = ψ(b) with b ∈ V₀ (step 4). Then Q(y) = Φ(b) and Θ(Q(y)) = b, so f(y) = g(Θ(Q(y))). Thus f agrees with g∘Θ∘Q on M ∩ ball(ψ(a), δ), a neighbourhood of ψ(a) within M, and at ψ(a) itself. Suppose g is differentiable at a = Θ(Q(ψ(a))). Then g∘Θ∘Q is differentiable at ψ(a) by the chain rule, so f is differentiable within M at ψ(a) (HasFDerivWithinAt.congr_of_eventuallyEq).

6. (Rademacher in a chart.) g is locally Lipschitz on V. Let b ∈ V. By LocallyLipschitzOn, f is K-Lipschitz on M ∩ U for some neighbourhood U of ψ(b) and some K. Choose a closed ball B̄ ⊆ V around b with ψ(B̄) ⊆ U (continuity of ψ at b). On the compact convex set B̄, ψ is Λ-Lipschitz, where Λ := sup_{B̄} ‖Dψ‖ < ∞ (mean value inequality). Since ψ(B̄) ⊆ M ∩ U, g is KΛ-Lipschitz on B̄. Cover V by countably many open balls B_l whose closures B̄_l ⊆ V are such balls (second countability). On each B_l apply Rademacher's theorem in ℝ^m: LipschitzOnWith.ae_differentiableWithinAt_of_mem (Analysis/Calculus/Rademacher.lean:361), with μ = volume, an additive Haar measure. It shows that g is differentiable within B_l, hence at the point (B_l is open), at Lebesgue-a.e. point of B_l. So N_ψ := {b ∈ V : g is not differentiable at b} is Lebesgue-null.

7. (Lipschitz images of null sets are null.) On each B̄_l of step 6, ψ is Λ_l-Lipschitz. So μH[m](ψ(N_ψ ∩ B̄_l)) ≤ Λ_l^m·μH[m](N_ψ ∩ B̄_l) (LipschitzOnWith.hausdorffMeasure_image_le, MeasureTheory/Measure/Hausdorff.lean:733). On ℝ^m, μHE[m] = volume (EuclideanSpace.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_eq_volume, Geometry/Euclidean/Volume/Measure.lean:187), and μHE[m] is a positive multiple of μH[m]. Hence μH[m](N_ψ ∩ B̄_l) = 0, so μ(ψ(N_ψ ∩ B̄_l)) = 0, and μ(ψ(N_ψ)) ≤ Σ_l μ(ψ(N_ψ ∩ B̄_l)) = 0.

8. (Conclusion.) Let Bad := {x ∈ M : f is not differentiable within M at x}. Let x ∈ Bad and choose i with x ∈ W_i (step 2). Then x = ψ_i(a) with a ∈ V_i, and a ∈ N_{ψ_i} by step 5 (otherwise f would be differentiable within M at x). So Bad ⊆ ⋃_i ψ_i(N_{ψ_i}), and μ(Bad) = 0 by step 7 and countable subadditivity. Since M is Borel (step 2), ae_restrict_iff' turns this into ∀ᵐ x ∂(μHE[m].restrict M), DifferentiableWithinAt ℝ f M x. ∎
proof_key_steps: Charts are homeomorphisms onto W ∩ M (properness + injectivity); M = O ∩ closure(M) is Borel and countably many charts cover M.
Inverse function theorem for Q∘ψ (Q a left inverse of Dψ(a)) gives a local C¹ left inverse Θ∘Q of ψ on M near ψ(a), so f = (f∘ψ)∘Θ∘Q on M near ψ(a).
f∘ψ is locally Lipschitz on V, hence differentiable Lebesgue-a.e. (LipschitzOnWith.ae_differentiableWithinAt_of_mem); differentiability transfers to f within M.
ψ is locally Lipschitz and μHE[m] = volume on ℝ^m, so ψ maps Lebesgue-null sets to H^m-null sets (hausdorffMeasure_image_le); countable union over charts.

subproblem.title: Tangential derivatives are well defined: fderivWithin agrees with any derivative within M on span(tangentSpace M x)
subproblem.statement: Let P ∈ ℕ, E a real normed space, M ⊆ ℝ^P, f : ℝ^P → E, f' : ℝ^P →L[ℝ] E and x ∈ ℝ^P. If f has derivative f' within M at x (HasFDerivWithinAt f f' M x), then fderivWithin ℝ f M x v = f' v for every v in the linear span of tangentSpace M x (the velocities γ'(0) of curves γ, C¹ on (−1,1), with γ((−1,1)) ⊆ M and γ(0) = x).

Notation. T := tangentSpace M x, the set of velocities γ'(0) of maps γ : ℝ → ℝ^P that are C¹ on (−1,1), map (−1,1) into M and satisfy γ(0) = x. L₁ := fderivWithin ℝ f M x and L₂ := f', both continuous linear maps ℝ^P → E.

1. (Velocities lie in the tangent cone.) Let v ∈ T, witnessed by γ. For n ∈ ℕ put s_n := 1/(n + 2) ∈ (0, 1/2], c_n := n + 2 and d_n := γ(s_n) − x. Since s_n ∈ (−1,1), x + d_n = γ(s_n) ∈ M for every n. Since γ is differentiable, hence continuous, at 0 and s_n → 0, d_n → γ(0) − x = 0. Finally c_n·d_n = (γ(s_n) − γ(0))/s_n → v, because γ has derivative v at 0 and s_n → 0 with s_n ≠ 0. By the sequential criterion for the tangent cone (Mathlib mem_tangentConeAt_of_seq, Analysis/Calculus/TangentCone/Defs.lean:96, with the filter atTop on ℕ), v ∈ tangentConeAt ℝ M x. Hence T ⊆ tangentConeAt ℝ M x.

2. (fderivWithin is a derivative.) The hypothesis HasFDerivWithinAt f f' M x makes f differentiable within M at x. Therefore HasFDerivWithinAt f L₁ M x (Mathlib DifferentiableWithinAt.hasFDerivWithinAt, FDeriv/Basic.lean:391).

3. (Uniqueness on the tangent cone.) f has the two derivatives L₁ (step 2) and L₂ (hypothesis) within M at x. By HasFDerivWithinAt.unique_on they agree on tangentConeAt ℝ M x, and hence on T by step 1.

Hence fderivWithin ℝ f M x v = f' v for every v ∈ span T. (If x ∉ M then T = ∅ and the span is {0}, where the identity holds by linearity. The argument above covers this case as well.) ∎

subproblem.title: Tangent spaces of a hypersurface of A₀: T_xM = A₀ ∩ ν(x)^⊥ and P_x = Π_{A₀} − ν(x)⊗ν(x)
subproblem.statement: Let P, m ∈ ℕ, A₀ ⊆ ℝ^P a linear subspace with dim A₀ = m + 1, M ⊆ A₀ an embedded C¹ m-dimensional submanifold of ℝ^P (IsEmbeddedSubmanifold 1 m M), and ν : ℝ^P → ℝ^P with ν(x) ∈ A₀, |ν(x)| = 1 and ν(x)·v = 0 for all v ∈ tangentSpace M x, for every x ∈ M. Then for every x ∈ M: tangentSpace M x = {v ∈ A₀ : ν(x)·v = 0}, and for every w ∈ ℝ^P, (span tangentSpace M x).starProjection w = A₀.starProjection w − (ν(x)·w)ν(x).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P m : ℕ) (A₀ : Submodule ℝ (Euclid P)) (M : Set (Euclid P)) (ν : Euclid P → Euclid P), Module.finrank ℝ A₀ = m + 1 → M ⊆ (A₀ : Set (Euclid P)) → IsEmbeddedSubmanifold 1 m M → (∀ x ∈ M, ν x ∈ A₀ ∧ ‖ν x‖ = 1 ∧ ∀ v ∈ tangentSpace M x, inner ℝ (ν x) v = 0) → ∀ x ∈ M, tangentSpace M x = {v : Euclid P | v ∈ A₀ ∧ inner ℝ (ν x) v = 0} ∧ ∀ w : Euclid P, (Submodule.span ℝ (tangentSpace M x)).starProjection w = A₀.starProjection w - inner ℝ (ν x) w • ν x
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source. Parent proof (0b): "T_x is an m-dimensional linear subspace (chart_tangent_space), T_x ⊆ A₀ (velocities of curves in M ⊆ A₀), A₀ = T_x ⊕ ℝν(x) orthogonally". The projection formula is the explicit form of that orthogonal decomposition.

Fix x ∈ M. Write T := tangentSpace M x, H := {v ∈ ℝ^P : v ∈ A₀ and ν(x)·v = 0}, and Π := A₀.starProjection, the orthogonal projection onto A₀.

1. (T is an m-dimensional linear subspace.) IsEmbeddedSubmanifold 1 m M at the point x gives open V ⊆ ℝ^m and W ⊆ ℝ^P with x ∈ W, and a map ψ : ℝ^m → ℝ^P with the following properties: ψ is C¹ on V and injective on V; ψ(V) = W ∩ M; V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) is compact for every compact K ⊆ W; and Dψ(z) is injective for z ∈ V. Since x ∈ W ∩ M = ψ(V), we have x = ψ(v₀) with v₀ ∈ V. The accepted sibling chart_tangent_space (Submission.chart_tangentSpace_eq_range_fderiv, with r = 1 and N = M) gives T = range Dψ(v₀). So T is the range of an injective linear map ℝ^m → ℝ^P, hence a linear subspace of dimension m.

2. (T ⊆ A₀.) Let v ∈ T with witness γ (C¹ on (−1,1), γ((−1,1)) ⊆ M, γ(0) = x, γ'(0) = v). For 0 < |s| < 1, γ(s) and γ(0) lie in M ⊆ A₀, so the difference quotient (γ(s) − γ(0))/s lies in A₀. These quotients converge to v as s → 0. A₀ is finite-dimensional, hence closed, so v ∈ A₀.

3. (T ⊆ H.) Combine step 2 with the hypothesis ν(x)·v = 0 for v ∈ T.

4. (dim H = m.) H is the kernel of the linear functional λ : A₀ → ℝ, λ(w) := ν(x)·w. Since ν(x) ∈ A₀ and λ(ν(x)) = |ν(x)|² = 1, λ is surjective. By rank–nullity, dim H = dim A₀ − 1 = (m + 1) − 1 = m.

5. (T = H.) T ⊆ H are subspaces of the same finite dimension m (steps 1, 3, 4), so T = H (Submodule.eq_of_le_of_finrank_eq). This is the first claim, an equality of sets.

6. (Projection formula.) By step 5, span T = T = H. Fix w ∈ ℝ^P and put u := Πw − (ν(x)·w)ν(x).
 (a) u ∈ H. Πw and ν(x) lie in A₀, so u ∈ A₀. Also ν(x)·u = ν(x)·Πw − (ν(x)·w)|ν(x)|² = (Πν(x))·w − ν(x)·w = 0, because Π is self-adjoint and Πν(x) = ν(x) (ν(x) ∈ A₀).
 (b) w − u ⊥ H. Let h ∈ H ⊆ A₀. Then (w − Πw)·h = 0 since w − Πw ⊥ A₀, and ν(x)·h = 0. So (w − u)·h = (w − Πw)·h + (ν(x)·w)(ν(x)·h) = 0.
 The orthogonal projection onto the closed subspace H is the unique point u ∈ H with w − u ⊥ H (Mathlib Submodule.eq_starProjection_of_mem_of_inner_eq_zero). Therefore (Submodule.span ℝ T).starProjection w = u = Πw − (ν(x)·w)ν(x). ∎
proof_key_steps: A chart at x and chart_tangent_space give tangentSpace M x = range Dψ(v₀), an m-dimensional subspace.
Velocities of curves in M ⊆ A₀ lie in the closed subspace A₀, and they are ⊥ ν(x) by hypothesis.
A₀ ∩ ν(x)^⊥ has dimension m (rank–nullity, ν(x) ∈ A₀ a unit vector), so the inclusion is an equality.
u := Πw − (ν(x)·w)ν(x) lies in A₀ ∩ ν(x)^⊥ and w − u is orthogonal to it, so u is the orthogonal projection.

subproblem.title: Homogeneity of the tangent spaces and of the unit normal of a cone
subproblem.statement: Let P, m ∈ ℕ, A₀ ⊆ ℝ^P a subspace with dim A₀ = m + 1, M ⊆ A₀ with IsEmbeddedSubmanifold 1 m M and tx ∈ M for all x ∈ M, t > 0; let ν : ℝ^P → ℝ^P be C^∞ on some open O ⊇ M, with ν(x) ∈ A₀, |ν(x)| = 1 and ν(x)·v = 0 for every v ∈ tangentSpace M x, for every x ∈ M. Then for every x ∈ M: x ∈ tangentSpace M x; Dν(x)x = 0; and for every t > 0: tangentSpace M (tx) = tangentSpace M x, ν(tx) = ν(x), and t·Dν(tx)v = Dν(x)v for every v ∈ tangentSpace M x.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P m : ℕ) (A₀ : Submodule ℝ (Euclid P)) (M : Set (Euclid P)) (ν : Euclid P → Euclid P), Module.finrank ℝ A₀ = m + 1 → M ⊆ (A₀ : Set (Euclid P)) → IsEmbeddedSubmanifold 1 m M → (∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → ∀ x ∈ M, t • x ∈ M) → (∃ O : Set (Euclid P), IsOpen O ∧ M ⊆ O ∧ ContDiffOn ℝ (⊤ : ℕ∞) ν O) → (∀ x ∈ M, ν x ∈ A₀ ∧ ‖ν x‖ = 1 ∧ ∀ v ∈ tangentSpace M x, inner ℝ (ν x) v = 0) → ∀ x ∈ M, x ∈ tangentSpace M x ∧ fderiv ℝ ν x x = 0 ∧ ∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → tangentSpace M (t • x) = tangentSpace M x ∧ ν (t • x) = ν x ∧ ∀ v ∈ tangentSpace M x, t • fderiv ℝ ν (t • x) v = fderiv ℝ ν x v
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source. Parent proof (0b) (x ∈ T_x via s ↦ e^s x; T_{tx} = T_x) and (0d) (homogeneity: ν(tx) = ν(x), t·Dν(tx)τ = Dν(x)τ, D_xν = 0), which is step 3 of the grandparent proof.

0. (Setting.) Fix an open O ⊇ M on which ν is C^∞. Then ν is continuous on O and differentiable at every point of O, and M ⊆ O. For y ∈ M write T_y := tangentSpace M y. By the sibling normal_complement (Submission.codim1_hcp_sc_tangent_normal_complement), T_y = {v ∈ A₀ : ν(y)·v = 0} for every y ∈ M. In particular each T_y is a linear subspace. Fix x ∈ M.

1. (x ∈ T_x.) Let γ(s) := e^s·x. γ is C^∞. For s ∈ (−1,1), γ(s) ∈ M by the cone property, since e^s > 0. Also γ(0) = x and γ'(0) = x. So x ∈ T_x.

2. (t·T_x ⊆ T_{tx}.) Let t > 0 and v ∈ T_x with witness γ. The curve tγ is C¹ on (−1,1) and maps (−1,1) into M (cone property). Moreover (tγ)(0) = tx and (tγ)'(0) = tv. So tv ∈ T_{tx}.

3. (T_{tx} = T_x.) Let t > 0. If v ∈ T_x then t⁻¹v ∈ T_x (subspace), so v = t·(t⁻¹v) ∈ T_{tx} by step 2. Conversely, tx ∈ M. Step 2 at the point tx with factor t⁻¹ gives t⁻¹w ∈ T_{t⁻¹·tx} = T_x for every w ∈ T_{tx}. Hence w ∈ T_x, since T_x is a subspace.

4. (ν(tx) = ±ν(x).) Let t > 0 and y := tx ∈ M. Then ν(y) ∈ A₀, and ν(y)·v = 0 for v ∈ T_y = T_x (step 3). Put λ := ν(x)·ν(y) and h := ν(y) − λν(x). Then h ∈ A₀ and ν(x)·h = λ − λ|ν(x)|² = 0, so h ∈ T_x by step 0. Hence |h|² = h·ν(y) − λ(h·ν(x)) = 0 − 0 = 0. So ν(y) = λν(x), and |λ| = |ν(y)| = 1, i.e. λ ∈ {−1, 1}.

5. (ν(tx) = ν(x).) Let g(t) := ν(tx)·ν(x) for t ∈ (0,∞). The map t ↦ tx is continuous with values in M ⊆ O, and ν is continuous on O, so g is continuous on (0,∞). By step 4, g takes values in {−1, 1}, and g(1) = 1. Suppose g(t₁) = −1 for some t₁ > 0. The closed interval between 1 and t₁ lies in (0,∞), and the intermediate value theorem gives t₂ there with g(t₂) = 0, which is impossible. So g ≡ 1, and ν(tx) = ν(x) for every t > 0 by step 4.

6. (t·Dν(tx)v = Dν(x)v.) Let t > 0 and v ∈ T_x with witness γ. For s ∈ (−1,1) we have γ(s) ∈ M, so step 5 at the point γ(s) gives ν(tγ(s)) = ν(γ(s)). The functions s ↦ ν(tγ(s)) and s ↦ ν(γ(s)) agree on the neighbourhood (−1,1) of 0. ν is differentiable at tγ(0) = tx and at γ(0) = x (both in O), and the inner maps have derivatives tv and v at 0. By the chain rule their derivatives at 0 are Dν(tx)(tv) and Dν(x)v. Functions agreeing near 0 have equal derivatives there, so t·Dν(tx)v = Dν(tx)(tv) = Dν(x)v.

7. (Dν(x)x = 0.) By step 5, t ↦ ν(tx) is constant (= ν(x)) on the open interval (0,∞), which contains 1. So its derivative at t = 1 is 0. By the chain rule (t ↦ tx has derivative x; ν is differentiable at x) this derivative is Dν(x)x. Hence fderiv ℝ ν x x = 0.

Steps 1, 7, 3, 5 and 6 are the five conjuncts of the conclusion. ∎
proof_key_steps: s ↦ e^s x is a C¹ curve in M through x with velocity x, so x ∈ T_x; tangent spaces are subspaces (normal_complement).
Scaling curves gives t·T_x ⊆ T_{tx}, and with linearity T_{tx} = T_x.
ν(tx) ∈ A₀ ∩ T_x^⊥ = ℝν(x) is a unit vector, so ν(tx) = ±ν(x); continuity in t on (0,∞) and IVT give ν(tx) = ν(x).
Differentiate ν(tγ(s)) = ν(γ(s)) at s = 0 along curves in M: t·Dν(tx)v = Dν(x)v.
Differentiate the constant map t ↦ ν(tx) at t = 1: Dν(x)x = 0.

Source. Parent proof (4c), integration by parts via stationarity and the Lipschitz approximation sibling (the grandparent's lipschitz_approx). The parent builds the vector field from graph charts and a partition of unity. Here the tangential gradient has the explicit ambient C¹ extension V := P̃∇F with P̃ := Π − ν⊗ν (normal_complement), so a single cut-off β replaces the partition of unity. The hypothesis (HL) is verbatim the conclusion of Submission.codim1_hcp_lipschitz_smooth_approx for M.

Notation. Fix the open O ⊇ M on which ν is C^∞, and f, F, O' as in the statement (F is C² on the open O' ⊇ M and F = f on M). Let μ := μHE[m] restricted to M (∫_M … dμ means ∫ x in M, … ∂μHE[m]). T_y := tangentSpace M y; P_y := orthogonal projection onto span T_y; e_j the standard basis. δ_jg(y) := fderivWithin ℝ g M y (P_ye_j). lap f(x) := Σ_jδ_j(δ_jf)(x). U := (O ∩ O') ∖ {0}, an open set containing M (0 ∉ M). Fix φ, locally Lipschitz on M, vanishing on M ∖ C with C ⊆ M compact.

1. (Smooth extensions.) By normal_complement, P_y = P̃(y) for y ∈ M, where P̃(y)w := Πw − (ν(y)·w)ν(y) is C^∞ on O. Put G_j(y) := DF(y)(P̃(y)e_j), C¹ on O ∩ O', and V(y) := Σ_j G_j(y)e_j. Then V is C¹ on O ∩ O', and for y ∈ M, V(y) = P_y∇F(y) ∈ T_y. Indeed G_j(y) = ∇F(y)·P_ye_j = P_y∇F(y)·e_j. By tangent_fderiv (F = f on M, F differentiable at y): δ_jf(y) = DF(y)(P_ye_j) = G_j(y) for y ∈ M. Applying it again to δ_jf = G_j on M: δ_j(δ_jf)(x) = DG_j(x)(P_xe_j). So δ_jf and lap f are continuous on M, being restrictions of continuous functions on O ∩ O'.

2. (Tangential derivatives of Lipschitz functions.) Let g be locally Lipschitz on M.
 (a) |δ_jg| is bounded on every compact K ⊆ M. Cover K by finitely many sets M ∩ U_l on which g is K_l-Lipschitz. If g is differentiable within M at y, then for τ ∈ T_y with witness γ, fderivWithin ℝ g M y τ = (g∘γ)'(0) (chain rule within M; γ maps into M), and |g(γ(s)) − g(y)| ≤ K_l|γ(s) − y|. Hence |fderivWithin ℝ g M y τ| ≤ K_l|τ|, so |δ_jg(y)| ≤ K_l since P_ye_j ∈ span T_y = T_y and |P_ye_j| ≤ 1. If g is not differentiable within M at y, then fderivWithin ℝ g M y = 0.
 (b) If g vanishes on M ∖ K for a compact K ⊆ M, then δ_jg = 0 on M ∖ K. M ∖ K is relatively open in M, so g vanishes on M near y. Hence g has derivative 0 within M at y, and tangent_fderiv applies.
 (c) δ_jg is μ-a.e. strongly measurable, by part (i) of (HL).

3. (Integrability.) M is a Borel set (hypothesis). Let K₀ := C; μ(K₀) < ∞ by local finiteness. The function x ↦ Σ_jδ_jφ(x)δ_jf(x) is a.e. strongly measurable (2(c), and δ_jf is continuous on M). It vanishes on M ∖ C (2(b)) and is bounded on C (2(a) and continuity of δ_jf on the compact C), so it is μ-integrable. Similarly φ·lap f is a.e. strongly measurable: φ is continuous on M, and lap f is continuous on M (step 1). It vanishes on M ∖ C and is bounded on C, so it is integrable. These are the first two conjuncts.

4. (Approximation.) By part (ii) of (HL) applied to φ, there are a compact C'' ⊆ M and C^∞ functions χ_k with compact support such that: χ_k = 0 on M ∖ C''; χ_k → φ uniformly on M; and ∫⁻_M Σ_j(Dχ_k(x)(P_xe_j) − δ_jφ(x))² dμ → 0. By tangent_fderiv, Dχ_k(x)(P_xe_j) = δ_jχ_k(x) for x ∈ M. Let K := C ∪ C'', a compact subset of M.

5. (Cut-off.) K is a compact subset of the open set U. Choose an open W₁ with K ⊆ W₁ and closure(W₁) ⊆ U compact, and a C^∞ function β : ℝ^P → [0, 1] with β = 1 on a neighbourhood of K and tsupport β ⊆ W₁. (Use Mathlib exists_contDiff_support_eq_eq_one_iff, Geometry/Manifold/PartitionOfUnity.lean:789, with s := W₁ and t := closure of an open W₂, K ⊆ W₂ ⊆ closure(W₂) ⊆ W₁.) Define X_k(z) := χ_k(z)β(z)V(z) for z ∈ U and X_k(z) := 0 otherwise. X_k is C¹ on U and vanishes on the open set ℝ^P ∖ tsupport β. These two open sets cover ℝ^P, so X_k is C¹ on ℝ^P. Its support lies in the compact set tsupport β ⊆ U, so X_k has compact support and 0 ∉ tsupport X_k.

6. (Tangential divergence of X_k.) For a C¹ field X and x ∈ M:
 trace(P_x∘DX(x)) = trace(DX(x)∘P_x) = Σ_j e_j·DX(x)(P_xe_j) = Σ_j δ_j(X·e_j)(x),
using cyclicity of the trace, the matrix of DX(x)∘P_x, and tangent_fderiv. Claim: for x ∈ M,
 trace(P_x∘DX_k(x)) = Σ_jδ_jχ_k(x)δ_jf(x) + χ_k(x)·lap f(x).
 (a) If x ∈ K, then β = 1 near x, so X_k = χ_kV near x and X_k·e_j = χ_kG_j there. By the product rule, D(χ_kG_j)(x)(P_xe_j) = Dχ_k(x)(P_xe_j)G_j(x) + χ_k(x)DG_j(x)(P_xe_j) = δ_jχ_k(x)δ_jf(x) + χ_k(x)δ_j(δ_jf)(x), by steps 1 and 4. Sum over j.
 (b) If x ∈ M ∖ K, then χ_k = 0 on the relatively open set M ∖ C'' ∋ x. So X_k·e_j and χ_k vanish on M near x, and their tangential derivatives at x vanish (2(b)). Both sides of the claim are 0 (χ_k(x) = 0).

7. (Stationarity.) X_k is C¹ with compact support and 0 ∉ tsupport X_k (step 5). The stationarity hypothesis and step 6 give ∫_M (Σ_jδ_jχ_kδ_jf + χ_k·lap f) dμ = 0 for every k. Both summands are integrable: they are continuous on M, zero on M ∖ K, and bounded on K.

8. (Limit.) Let B := sup_K (Σ_j(δ_jf)²)^{1/2} and L := sup_K|lap f|, both finite by continuity on the compact K. All functions below vanish on M ∖ K. By Cauchy–Schwarz in j and then in L²(μ⌞K):
 ∫_M|Σ_j(δ_jχ_k − δ_jφ)δ_jf| dμ ≤ B·μ(K)^{1/2}·(∫_M Σ_j(δ_jχ_k − δ_jφ)² dμ)^{1/2} → 0, by step 4;
 ∫_M|χ_k − φ|·|lap f| dμ ≤ L·μ(K)·sup_M|χ_k − φ| → 0.
 Hence ∫_M(Σ_jδ_jφδ_jf + φ·lap f) dμ = lim_k ∫_M(Σ_jδ_jχ_kδ_jf + χ_k·lap f) dμ = 0. By step 3 both summands are integrable, so the integral splits:
 ∫_M Σ_jδ_jφδ_jf dμ = −∫_M φ·lap f dμ.
This is the third conjunct, and with step 3 the proof is complete. ∎

Tangential derivatives of locally Lipschitz functions are bounded on compacts, vanish off the support, and are measurable by (HL)(i): integrability.
(HL)(ii) approximants χ_k and a cut-off β give X_k := χ_kβV, C¹ with compact support avoiding 0; div_M X_k = Σ_jδ_jχ_kδ_jf + χ_kΔ_Mf on M.

subproblem.title: A minimal hypercone with the Hardy-type inequality (3), 2 ≤ m ≤ 6, has vanishing second fundamental form (end of the proof of Simon B.2)
subproblem.statement: Let P, m ∈ ℕ with 2 ≤ m ≤ 6, A₀ ⊆ ℝ^P a subspace with dim A₀ = m + 1, M ⊆ A₀ with 0 ∉ M, IsEmbeddedSubmanifold r m M for every r ∈ ℕ, closure(M) ⊆ M ∪ {0}, tx ∈ M for x ∈ M and t > 0, H^m(M ∩ K) < ∞ for compact K; let ν : ℝ^P → ℝ^P be C^∞ on some open O ⊇ M, with ν(x) ∈ A₀, |ν(x)| = 1 and ν(x)·v = 0 for every v ∈ tangentSpace M x, for every x ∈ M. Assume density one: for every z ∈ M, H^m(M ∩ B_s(z))/(ω_m s^m) → 1 as s ↓ 0 (ω_m = unitBallVolume m); and (H3): 2∫_M ψ²|A|²/|x|² dH^m ≤ ∫_M |A|²·Σ_j(δ_jψ)² dH^m for every ψ locally Lipschitz on M vanishing on M outside a compact subset of M. subproblem.natural_proof:
Source. Simon Appendix B, proof of B.2 after (3) (chapter-B.txt lines 250–282: the extension of (3) under (4), the cut-offs γ_ε, the polar formula (5) and the choice (6)), as in steps 5–7 of the parent proof. Documented departures, inherited from the parent proof: (i) the finiteness statements obtained in print from the polar formula (5) are obtained from the dyadic estimates of the sibling cone_measure; (iii) the printed cut-off parameter ε is called κ. Here (3) for compactly supported test functions is the hypothesis (H3); the parent obtains it from the sibling simons_hardy. The exponent ε = 1/10 is the witness of SimonGMT AppendixB.exists_final_exponent.

Notation. μ := μHE[m], with ∫_M … dμ meaning ∫ x in M, … ∂μHE[m]. r(x) := |x|. T_x := tangentSpace M x; P_x := orthogonal projection onto span T_x; e_j the standard basis; δ_jg(x) := fderivWithin ℝ g M x (P_xe_j). |A|²(x) := Σ_j|Dν(x)(P_xe_j)|². Fix the open O ⊇ M on which ν is C^∞. If M = ∅ there is nothing to prove; assume M ≠ ∅.

1. (Cone facts.)
 (a) tM = M for t > 0 (apply the cone property with t and t⁻¹). M = closure(M) ∖ {0} is Borel, because 0 ∉ M and closure(M) ⊆ M ∪ {0}. For 0 < a ≤ b, M ∩ {a ≤ r ≤ b} = closure(M) ∩ {a ≤ r ≤ b} is closed and bounded, hence compact.
 (b) By normal_complement, T_x = A₀ ∩ ν(x)^⊥ is a linear subspace for x ∈ M (so span T_x = T_x), and P_x = P̃(x) := Π − ν(x)⊗ν(x), where Π is the projection onto A₀. Hence |A|² = Ã on M with Ã(y) := Σ_j|Dν(y)(P̃(y)e_j)|², which is continuous on O. So |A|² is continuous on M, and |A|² ≥ 0.
 (c) By cone_normal (with IsEmbeddedSubmanifold 1 m M): for x ∈ M and t > 0, x ∈ T_x, T_{tx} = T_x (so P_{tx} = P_x), and t·Dν(tx)v = Dν(x)v for v ∈ T_x.
 (d) Homogeneity: |A|²(tx) = t⁻²|A|²(x) for x ∈ M and t > 0. Indeed |A|²(tx) = Σ_j|Dν(tx)(P_xe_j)|² = Σ_j|t⁻¹Dν(x)(P_xe_j)|², since P_xe_j ∈ T_x.
 (e) Bound: Σ₁ := M ∩ {r = 1} is compact by (a). Let c_Σ := max_{Σ₁}|A|² if Σ₁ ≠ ∅ and c_Σ := 0 otherwise. For x ∈ M, x/r(x) ∈ Σ₁ by the cone property, so |A|²(x) = r(x)⁻²|A|²(x/r(x)) ≤ c_Σ·r(x)⁻² by (d).

2. (Radial test functions.) Let u : (0,∞) → ℝ be differentiable at ρ₀ = r(x), x ∈ M, and let φ(y) := u(r(y)) for y ≠ 0. Then Σ_j(δ_jφ(x))² = u'(r(x))². Indeed φ is differentiable at x with Dφ(x)v = u'(r(x))·(x/r(x))·v, because the norm is differentiable away from 0. By tangent_fderiv, δ_jφ(x) = Dφ(x)(P_xe_j) = u'(r(x))·(x/r(x))·P_xe_j = u'(r(x))·(P_x(x/r(x)))·e_j = u'(r(x))·(x/r(x))·e_j, since P_x is self-adjoint and P_xx = x (x ∈ T_x). Finally Σ_j((x/r(x))·e_j)² = |x/r(x)|² = 1.

3. (Measure facts.) By cone_measure: (i) μ(M ∩ {r = c}) = 0 for every c > 0; (ii) ∫⁻_{M∩{r<1}} r^α dμ < ∞ for α > −m; (iii) ∫⁻_{M∖{r<1}} r^β dμ < ∞ for β < −m.

4. (The profile.) ε := 1/10. Let p(ρ) := ρ^{1+ε} for 0 < ρ ≤ 1 and p(ρ) := ρ^{2−m/2−ε} for ρ ≥ 1. This is ρ^{1+ε}·max(1, ρ)^{1−m/2−2ε}, the printed ψ = r^{1+ε}r₁^{1−n/2−2ε}. p is continuous, with p(1) = 1, and C^∞ on (0, 1) and on (1, ∞). There p'(ρ) = (1 + ε)ρ^ε and p'(ρ) = (2 − m/2 − ε)ρ^{1−m/2−ε} respectively. Hence p(ρ)²/ρ² = ρ^{2ε} on (0, 1) and ρ^{2−m−2ε} on (1, ∞), and p'(ρ)² = (1 + ε)²ρ^{2ε} on (0, 1) and (m/2 − 2 + ε)²ρ^{2−m−2ε} on (1, ∞).

5. (Finiteness, replacing (5).) Put I₁ := ∫_{M∩{r<1}} |A|²r^{2ε} dμ and I₂ := ∫_{M∩{r>1}} |A|²r^{2−m−2ε} dμ. The integrands are nonnegative and continuous on M, hence measurable. By 1(e), |A|²r^{2ε} ≤ c_Σr^{2ε−2}, and 2ε − 2 > −m because m ≥ 2 and ε > 0; so 3(ii) gives I₁ < ∞. Likewise |A|²r^{2−m−2ε} ≤ c_Σr^{−m−2ε}, and −m − 2ε < −m; so 3(iii) gives I₂ < ∞ (note {r > 1} ⊆ {r ≥ 1}). Since M ∩ {r = 1} is null (3(i)):
 J := ∫_M p(r)²|A|²/r² dμ = I₁ + I₂ < ∞,   K := ∫_M |A|²p'(r)² dμ = (1 + ε)²I₁ + (m/2 − 2 + ε)²I₂ < ∞.
 Here p'(r) is defined off the null set {r = 1}. Both integrands are integrable. This is the printed (4) for ψ = p(r).

6. (Cut-offs.) For 0 < κ < 1 let g_κ : [0, ∞) → [0, 1] be continuous and piecewise linear: 0 on [0, κ/2]; (2/κ)(ρ − κ/2) on [κ/2, κ]; 1 on [κ, κ⁻¹]; 2 − κρ on [κ⁻¹, 2κ⁻¹]; 0 on [2κ⁻¹, ∞). The breakpoints are ordered because κ < 1. Off the breakpoints, |g_κ'(ρ)| ≤ 3ρ⁻¹·1_{E_κ}(ρ) with E_κ := (κ/2, κ) ∪ (κ⁻¹, 2κ⁻¹). On (κ/2, κ), |g_κ'| = 2/κ < 2/ρ ≤ 3/ρ; on (κ⁻¹, 2κ⁻¹), |g_κ'| = κ < 2/ρ ≤ 3/ρ (the constant 3 is the printed one; 2 would do). Put u_κ := p·g_κ on (0, ∞) and φ_κ(y) := u_κ(r(y)) for y ≠ 0, φ_κ(0) := 0.
 (a) φ_κ is Lipschitz on ℝ^P, hence locally Lipschitz on M. u_κ vanishes on (0, κ/2] and on [2κ⁻¹, ∞). On [κ/2, 2κ⁻¹] it is continuous and piecewise C¹ with finitely many pieces and bounded derivative, so u_κ is Lipschitz on (0, ∞), and φ_κ = u_κ∘r with r 1-Lipschitz.
 (b) φ_κ vanishes on M outside C_κ := M ∩ {κ/2 ≤ r ≤ 2κ⁻¹}, a compact subset of M by 1(a).
 (c) By the hypothesis (H3) applied to φ_κ: 2∫_M φ_κ²|A|²/r² dμ ≤ ∫_M |A|²·Σ_j(δ_jφ_κ)² dμ.
 (d) Let Z_κ := M ∩ {r ∈ {κ/2, κ, 1, κ⁻¹, 2κ⁻¹}}, which is μ-null by 3(i). For x ∈ M ∖ Z_κ, u_κ is C¹ near r(x). By step 2, Σ_j(δ_jφ_κ(x))² = u_κ'(r)² = (p'g_κ + pg_κ')²(r). Fix η > 0. Using (a + b)² ≤ (1 + η)a² + (1 + η⁻¹)b², 0 ≤ g_κ ≤ 1 and the bound on g_κ':
 Σ_j(δ_jφ_κ(x))² ≤ (1 + η)p'(r)² + 9(1 + η⁻¹)·1_{E_κ}(r)·p(r)²/r².
 (e) Multiply by |A|² ≥ 0 and integrate. By (d), off the null set Z_κ, |A|²·Σ_j(δ_jφ_κ)² equals |A|²·u_κ'(r)², a bounded Borel function supported in the compact set C_κ. So it is integrable, and so is the right side (step 5). Then
 2∫_M g_κ(r)²p(r)²|A|²/r² dμ ≤ (1 + η)K + 9(1 + η⁻¹)∫_M 1_{E_κ}(r)p(r)²|A|²/r² dμ,
 because φ_κ² = g_κ(r)²p(r)².

7. (κ → 0.) Let κ_n := 1/(n + 2). For x ∈ M, 0 < r(x) < ∞. So for n large, κ_n < r(x) < κ_n⁻¹, giving g_{κ_n}(r(x)) = 1 and 1_{E_{κ_n}}(r(x)) = 0. Both integrands in 6(e) are dominated by the integrable function p(r)²|A|²/r² (step 5). By dominated convergence (tendsto_integral_of_dominated_convergence) the left side tends to 2J and the last integral tends to 0. Hence 2J ≤ (1 + η)K for every η > 0, and letting η → 0, 2J ≤ K. This is the printed (6).

8. (Choice of ε.) Step 7 reads 2(I₁ + I₂) ≤ (1 + ε)²I₁ + (m/2 − 2 + ε)²I₂, i.e.
 (2 − (1 + ε)²)I₁ + (2 − (m/2 − 2 + ε)²)I₂ ≤ 0.
 With ε = 1/10: (1 + ε)² = 1.21 < 2. For m ∈ {2, …, 6}, m/2 − 2 + ε ∈ {−0.9, −0.4, 0.1, 0.6, 1.1}, so (m/2 − 2 + ε)² ≤ 1.21 < 2. Both coefficients are positive and I₁, I₂ ∈ [0, ∞), so I₁ = I₂ = 0.

9. (|A|² = 0 a.e.) I₁ = 0 and r^{2ε} > 0 give |A|² = 0 μ-a.e. on M ∩ {r < 1}; similarly I₂ = 0 gives it on M ∩ {r > 1}. M ∩ {r = 1} is null (3(i)). So |A|² = 0 μ-a.e. on M.

subproblem.natural_proof:
Source. Simon Appendix B, B.4–B.9 (chapter-B.txt lines 88–160), as organized in step 1 of the parent proof. Parent (0c) and (0g) supply the bridge between the frame-free Lean quantities and the frame components. Documented erratum: as printed, the second line of B.7 carries the opposite sign on the two curvature terms relative to its first line and to B.6. One fixed convention is used below (II.4), and the result coincides with the printed B.8.

Notation. Fix an open O ⊇ M on which ν is C^∞. T_y := tangentSpace M y; P_y := orthogonal projection onto span T_y; e_1, …, e_P the standard basis; Π := orthogonal projection onto A₀. |A|²(y) := Σ_i |Dν(y)(P_ye_i)|². δ_jg(y) := fderivWithin ℝ g M y (P_ye_j) and Δ_Mg(x) := Σ_j δ_j(δ_jg)(x). C(y) := Dν(y)∘P_y and D_aC := fderivWithin ℝ C M x a. |∇A|²(x) := Σ_{i,j,k} ((D_{P_xe_k}C)(P_xe_i)·P_xe_j)². The claim is Δ_M|A|²(x) = 2|∇A|²(x) − 2(|A|²(x))² for x ∈ M.

Part I. Ambient extensions, a frame, and three bridges.

I.1 (Extensions.) P̃(y)w := Πw − (ν(y)·w)ν(y), C̃(y) := Dν(y)∘P̃(y) and Ã(y) := Σ_i |C̃(y)e_i|² are C^∞ on O (Dν is C^∞ on the open O by ContDiffOn.fderiv_of_isOpen). By the sibling normal_complement, for y ∈ M: T_y = A₀ ∩ ν(y)^⊥ (a subspace) and P_y = P̃(y). Hence C = C̃ and |A|² = Ã on M.
 Extension principle (E). Let g : ℝ^P → F agree on M ∩ U (U an open neighbourhood of y ∈ M) with a function G differentiable at y. Then fderivWithin ℝ g M y τ = DG(y)τ for every τ ∈ T_y. Reason: g has derivative DG(y) within M at y (congruence on M ∩ U; fderivWithin is local, fderivWithin_inter); now apply the sibling tangent_fderiv.
 Consequently δ_j|A|² = G_j on M with G_j(y) := DÃ(y)(P̃(y)e_j), and Δ_M|A|²(x) = Σ_j DG_j(x)(P_xe_j). Also D_aC = DC̃(x)a for a ∈ T_x.

I.2 (Second fundamental form.) By the sibling codazzi, for y ∈ M and a, b, d ∈ T_y: Dν(y)a ∈ T_y; Dν(y)a·b = Dν(y)b·a; and (D_aC)(b)·d is symmetric in (a, b) and in (b, d).

I.3 (Frame.) Fix x₀ ∈ M. The vectors P_{x₀}e_1, …, P_{x₀}e_P span T_{x₀}, which has dimension m. Choose j_1, …, j_m with P_{x₀}e_{j_1}, …, P_{x₀}e_{j_m} linearly independent. P̃ is continuous, so there is an open ball B ⊆ O around x₀ on which w_a(y) := P̃(y)e_{j_a} (a = 1, …, m) are linearly independent. Gram–Schmidt gives C^∞ maps E_1, …, E_m : B → ℝ^P, orthonormal at every y ∈ B, with span{E_a(y)} = span{w_a(y)}. For y ∈ M ∩ B, w_a(y) ∈ T_y and dim T_y = m. So (E_a(y))_a is an orthonormal basis of T_y.

I.4 (Tangent fields; connection.) A tangent field is a C^∞ map X : B → ℝ^P with X(y) ∈ T_y for y ∈ M ∩ B; examples are E_a and Σ_a f_aE_a with f_a C^∞. For a tangent field X and a C¹ map Z on B put D_XZ(y) := DZ(y)X(y). By (E), D_XZ at points of M ∩ B depends only on Z restricted to M ∩ B. Define ∇_XY := P(D_XY) and [X, Y] := D_XY − D_YX.
 (a) Gauss formula. For tangent X, Y and y ∈ M ∩ B: D_XY ∈ A₀. Indeed, let γ witness X(y) ∈ T_y. Then Y∘γ takes values in A₀ near s = 0 (Y(z) ∈ T_z ⊆ A₀ for z ∈ M). Its derivative at 0 is DY(y)X(y) = D_XY(y). The difference quotients lie in the closed subspace A₀, so D_XY(y) ∈ A₀. Also ν·D_XY = −Dν(X)·Y: differentiate ν·Y, which vanishes on M ∩ B, along X and use (E). Since A₀ = T_y ⊕ ℝν(y) orthogonally, D_XY = ∇_XY + h(X, Y)ν with h(X, Y) := −Dν(X)·Y = SX·Y, where SX := −Dν(X) is tangent (I.2). h is symmetric (I.2).
 (b) Torsion-freeness. ν·[X, Y] = h(X, Y) − h(Y, X) = 0 and [X, Y] ∈ A₀, so [X, Y] is tangent and ∇_XY − ∇_YX = P[X, Y] = [X, Y].
 (c) Metric compatibility. X(Y·Z) = ∇_XY·Z + Y·∇_XZ for tangent Y, Z. Indeed X(Y·Z) = D_XY·Z + Y·D_XZ, and only tangential parts pair with tangent vectors.
 (d) Flatness. For tangent X, Y and a C² map Z on B: D_XD_YZ − D_YD_XZ − D_{[X,Y]}Z = 0 on M ∩ B. This follows from D_X(DZ·Y) − D_Y(DZ·X) = D²Z(X, Y) + DZ(D_XY) − D²Z(Y, X) − DZ(D_YX) = DZ([X, Y]), using symmetry of D²Z (ContDiffAt.isSymmSndFDerivAt). Applied to scalar functions f, this gives XYf − YXf = [X, Y]f.

I.5 (Covariant derivatives in the frame.) Indices a, b, c, … run over 1, …, m and repeated indices are summed. For functions f on M ∩ B put E_cf := D_{E_c}f. Define:
 h_ab := h(E_a, E_b);
 h_{ab;c} := E_c(h_ab) − h(∇_{E_c}E_a, E_b) − h(E_a, ∇_{E_c}E_b);
 h_{ab;cd} := E_d(h_{ab;c}) − (∇h)(∇_{E_d}E_a, E_b, E_c) − (∇h)(E_a, ∇_{E_d}E_b, E_c) − (∇h)(E_a, E_b, ∇_{E_d}E_c), so the index c is differentiated first;
 f_{;c} := E_cf and f_{;cd} := E_d(E_cf) − (∇_{E_d}E_c)f;
 H := h_aa.
All are C^∞ functions on M ∩ B (restrictions of ambient C^∞ functions).

I.6 (Bridges.) At points of M ∩ B:
 (B1) h_{ab;c} = −(D_{E_c}C)(E_a)·E_b, and |∇A|² = Σ_{a,b,c} h_{ab;c}². For the first claim, h(X, Y) = −C X·Y for tangent X, Y, so E_c(h_ab) = −(D_{E_c}C)E_a·E_b − C(D_{E_c}E_a)·E_b − CE_a·D_{E_c}E_b. C kills normal components (C(y)w = Dν(y)(P_yw)), so C(D_{E_c}E_a) = C(∇_{E_c}E_a). CE_a is tangent (I.2), so CE_a·D_{E_c}E_b = CE_a·∇_{E_c}E_b. This gives the formula. For the second claim, use the Hilbert–Schmidt identity: for a linear functional ℓ on ℝ^P, Σ_jℓ(P_ye_j)² = Σ_aℓ(E_a)². Indeed P_ye_j = Σ_a(e_j·E_a)E_a and Σ_j(e_j·E_a)(e_j·E_b) = E_a·E_b = δ_ab. Apply it in each slot of the trilinear form (u, v, w) ↦ (D_{P_yu}C)(P_yv)·P_yw (D_·C is linear in the direction, by I.1).
 (B2) |A|² = h_ab h_ab. |A|²(y) = Σ_j|Dν(y)(P_ye_j)|² = Σ_a|Dν(y)E_a|², by the Hilbert–Schmidt identity for the linear map Dν(y). Then Σ_a|Dν(y)E_a|² = Σ_{a,b}(Dν(y)E_a·E_b)² because Dν(y)E_a ∈ T_y (Parseval).
 (B3) Δ_M|A|² = (|A|²)_{;cc}. Let g := |A|² and ∇g := (E_ag)E_a, a tangent field. For y ∈ M ∩ B, δ_jg(y) = Σ_a(e_j·E_a)E_ag = ∇g·e_j, by linearity of fderivWithin and P_ye_j = Σ_a(e_j·E_a)E_a. By (E), δ_j(δ_jg)(x₀) = D(∇g·e_j)(x₀)(P_{x₀}e_j) = (D_{P_{x₀}e_j}∇g)·e_j. Summing over j gives the trace of the linear map L∘P_{x₀}, where L := D(∇g)(x₀). This trace equals Σ_c(LE_c)·E_c, since L∘P_{x₀} vanishes on T_{x₀}^⊥. Moreover (LE_c)·E_c = (∇_{E_c}∇g)·E_c = E_c(∇g·E_c) − ∇g·∇_{E_c}E_c = E_c(E_cg) − (∇_{E_c}E_c)g = g_{;cc}, by (c) of I.4.

Part II. The intrinsic computation (Simon B.4–B.9, parent step 1), at points of M ∩ B.
II.1 (B.4) h_ab = h_ba (I.2). Hence h_{ab;c} and h_{ab;cd} are symmetric in a, b.
II.2 (Codazzi, B.5) h_{ab;c} is totally symmetric: by (B1), h_{ab;c} = −(D_{E_c}C)(E_a)·E_b, and I.2 gives symmetry in (c, a) and in (a, b).
II.3 (Gauss, B.6) R(X, Y)Z := ∇_X∇_YZ − ∇_Y∇_XZ − ∇_{[X,Y]}Z = h(Y, Z)SX − h(X, Z)SY for tangent X, Y, Z. Expand I.4(d) with D_YZ = ∇_YZ + h(Y, Z)ν and D_Xν = −SX: D_X(D_YZ) = ∇_X∇_YZ + h(X, ∇_YZ)ν + X(h(Y, Z))ν − h(Y, Z)SX. Do the same with X and Y exchanged, and use D_{[X,Y]}Z = ∇_{[X,Y]}Z + h([X, Y], Z)ν. The tangential component of I.4(d) is the Gauss equation. In components, R(E_a, E_b)E_c·E_d = h_bc h_ad − h_ac h_bd.
II.4 (Ricci identity, B.7, fixed convention) h_{ab;cd} − h_{ab;dc} = −h(R(E_d, E_c)E_a, E_b) − h(E_a, R(E_d, E_c)E_b). Here h_{ab;cd} = (∇²_{E_d,E_c}h)(E_a, E_b) with ∇²_{X,Y} := ∇_X∇_Y − ∇_{∇_XY}. Expand the definitions and use torsion-freeness ∇_XY − ∇_YX = [X, Y] (I.4(b)): ∇²_{X,Y}h − ∇²_{Y,X}h = ∇_X∇_Yh − ∇_Y∇_Xh − ∇_{[X,Y]}h. Evaluated on (U, W), the terms in which the operators act on the function h(U, W) cancel, because XYf − YXf − [X, Y]f = 0 (I.4(d)). The remaining terms are −h(R(X, Y)U, W) − h(U, R(X, Y)W).
II.5 (Commutation) Write SE_a = h_abE_b, (h²)_ab = h_ach_cb, (h³)_ab = h_ach_cdh_db (symmetric) and |A|² = h_abh_ab. Then
 Σ_c(h_{ca;bc} − h_{ca;cb}) = −h(R(E_c, E_b)E_c, E_a) − h(E_c, R(E_c, E_b)E_a)   [II.4 with (a, b, c, d) ↦ (c, a, b, c)]
 = −[(h³)_ba − H(h²)_ba] − [|A|²h_ba − (h³)_ab] = H(h²)_ab − |A|²h_ab.
 Here Gauss gives R(E_c, E_b)E_c = h_bcSE_c − h_ccSE_b, so h(R(E_c, E_b)E_c, E_a) = (h³)_ba − H(h²)_ba. Likewise R(E_c, E_b)E_a = h_baSE_c − h_caSE_b, so h(E_c, R(E_c, E_b)E_a) = |A|²h_ba − (h³)_ab.
II.6 (Laplacian of h) h_{ab;cc} = h_{ac;bc} (Codazzi II.2: the 3-tensors (a, b, c) ↦ h_{ab;c} and (a, b, c) ↦ h_{ac;b} coincide, hence so do their covariant derivatives) = h_{ca;bc} (II.1) = h_{ca;cb} + H(h²)_ab − |A|²h_ab (II.5) = H_{;ab} + H(h²)_ab − |A|²h_ab. For the last step, Σ_ch_{ca;c} = Σ_ch_{cc;a} = H_{;a} by Codazzi, because contraction commutes with ∇ for the orthonormal frame; hence Σ_ch_{ca;cb} = H_{;ab}.
II.7 (B.8) By metric compatibility, (|A|²)_{;c} = 2h_abh_{ab;c} and ½(|A|²)_{;cc} = h_{ab;c}h_{ab;c} + h_abh_{ab;cc}. With II.6:
 ½(|A|²)_{;cc} = Σ h²_{ab;c} − |A|⁴ + h_abH_{;ab} + H h_ab(h²)_ab.
II.8 (H = 0) H = h_aa = −Σ_aDν(y)E_a·E_a = −trace(Dν(y)∘P_y) = −trace(P_y∘Dν(y)) = 0 for every y ∈ M ∩ B, by hypothesis (trace is cyclic).  (c) Tangential derivatives of a function g that is locally Lipschitz on M. By tangent_fderiv, whenever g has derivative g' within M at x, δ_jg(x) = g'(P_xe_j), since P_xe_j ∈ span tangentSpace M x.
  (c1) δ_jg is bounded on every compact K ⊆ M. Cover K by finitely many sets M ∩ U_l on which g is K_l-Lipschitz.
